title: Jeremiah 32:1–15
context: Jeremiah 32:1–15 is set in the tenth year of Zedekiah, the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, while Babylon’s army besieges Jerusalem. The narrator explains that Jeremiah is confined in the court of the guard because Zedekiah objected to his prophecy that the city would fall and the king would be taken to Babylon. Jeremiah then tells in his own words how the LORD said that his cousin Hanamel would come and ask him to buy a field at Anathoth by the right of redemption. When Hanamel came, Jeremiah knew this was the LORD’s word. He paid seventeen shekels of silver, commonly reckoned at roughly 190–200 grams (about 7 ounces), signed and sealed the deed before witnesses, and gave both the sealed and open copies to Baruch to store in a clay jar. The LORD of Armies explains the sign: houses, fields, and vineyards will again be bought in this land. The siege and fall are also narrated in Jeremiah 39 and 52 and 2 Kings 25; the sign looks past that disaster to a future return.

verses.text: This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator dates this word to the tenth year of Zedekiah, the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar. Arminian readers see the setting as essential: God’s promise of a future comes at the darkest moment, just before Jerusalem falls.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the precise date as grounding the prophecy in real history. Both traditions note that the siege is also recorded in 2 Kings 25:1–2 and Jeremiah 39:1 and 52:4–5, and they read this chapter against that background.

verses.text: Now at that time the king of Babylon’s army was besieging Jerusalem. Jeremiah the prophet was shut up in the court of the guard, which was in the king of Judah’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator says Babylon’s army is besieging Jerusalem and Jeremiah is shut up in the court of the guard in the palace. Arminians see the prophet suffering for his faithfulness, confined by the king he warned.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s servant restricted yet still used to speak God’s word. Both traditions note that Jeremiah’s confinement in the court of the guard is also described in 37:21 and 38:28.

verses.text: For Zedekiah king of Judah had shut him up, saying, “Why do you prophesy, and say, ‘The LORD says, “Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will take it;
verses.arminianNotes: Zedekiah demands why Jeremiah prophesies that the LORD will give the city to the king of Babylon. Arminian readers see a king who resents God’s message rather than heeding it, though the warning still gave him room to respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the king’s resistance to God’s word. Both traditions read the verse as Zedekiah’s words, quoting Jeremiah’s message as the reason for his confinement, and they compare the fuller accounts in chapters 37–38.

verses.text: and Zedekiah king of Judah won’t escape out of the hand of the Chaldeans, but will surely be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon, and will speak with him mouth to mouth, and his eyes will see his eyes;
verses.arminianNotes: Zedekiah’s quotation continues: he will not escape but will be handed to the king of Babylon and see him face to face. Arminians see a specific warning given to the king, who could have responded with humility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the certainty of God’s word against the king. Both traditions note that Zedekiah’s capture is narrated in Jeremiah 39:5–7, 52:8–11, and 2 Kings 25:5–7, which are named here without harmonizing their details.

verses.text: and he will bring Zedekiah to Babylon, and he will be there until I visit him,” says the LORD, “though you fight with the Chaldeans, you will not prosper” ’?”
verses.arminianNotes: Zedekiah’s quotation ends: the king will be taken to Babylon until the LORD visits him, and fighting the Chaldeans will not succeed. Arminian readers see God’s warning that resistance is futile, which the prophet consistently urged on the king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign plan for the outcome of the siege. Both traditions note that the phrase until I visit him is not explained here, and they avoid reading more into it than the text says.

verses.text: Jeremiah said, “The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah begins to tell in his own words how the LORD’s word came to him. Arminians see the prophet as a faithful witness who reports his experience so that others can see God at work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the shift to first-person narration as making the account personal. Both traditions read what follows as Jeremiah’s report of a word he received and then saw confirmed.

verses.text: ‘Behold, Hanamel the son of Shallum your uncle will come to you, saying, “Buy my field that is in Anathoth; for the right of redemption is yours to buy it.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jeremiah that his cousin Hanamel will come and ask him to buy his field at Anathoth by the right of redemption. Arminian readers see God preparing his servant ahead of time, so that he will recognize the request when it comes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s foreknowledge in announcing Hanamel’s visit. Both traditions note that the right of redemption reflects the law’s concern to keep land within the family (Leviticus 25:25), and that Anathoth was Jeremiah’s hometown (1:1).

verses.text: “So Hanamel my uncle’s son came to me in the court of the guard according to the LORD’s word, and said to me, ‘Please buy my field that is in Anathoth, which is in the land of Benjamin; for the right of inheritance is yours, and the redemption is yours. Buy it for yourself.’ “Then I knew that this was the LORD’s word.
verses.arminianNotes: Hanamel comes as the LORD said and asks Jeremiah to buy the field, and Jeremiah knows it is the LORD’s word. Arminians see God confirming his word through events, which strengthens his servant’s confidence to act.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the fulfillment of God’s word as confirming its truth. Both traditions note that Jeremiah recognizes the LORD’s word through the event, and they read his knowledge as faith grounded in what God had said.

verses.text: I bought the field that was in Anathoth of Hanamel my uncle’s son, and weighed him the money, even seventeen shekels of silver.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah buys the field from Hanamel and weighs out seventeen shekels of silver, commonly reckoned at roughly 190–200 grams (about 7 ounces). Arminian readers see an act of faith that makes little sense economically, since the land is under enemy control.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see Jeremiah’s obedience as a public sign of God’s promise. Both traditions note that the price is real and modest, and they read the purchase as costly obedience rather than a shrewd investment.

verses.text: I signed the deed, sealed it, called witnesses, and weighed the money in the balances to him.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah signs and seals the deed, calls witnesses, and weighs the money on scales. Arminians see the care taken to make the transaction legal and public, so that the sign would be clear to all who saw it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the detailed legal steps as giving the sign weight and permanence. Both traditions read the verse as showing that God’s promise is meant to be taken seriously, as seriously as a legal contract.

verses.text: So I took the deed of the purchase, both that which was sealed, containing the terms and conditions, and that which was open;
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah takes the sealed deed with its terms and the open copy. Arminian readers see an ancient practice of keeping a sealed copy for security and an open copy for reference, which helps make the purchase secure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the two copies as standard legal practice of the time. Both traditions hold the specific details of the custom loosely, and agree on its main point: the purchase was properly recorded.

verses.text: and I delivered the deed of the purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah, the son of Mahseiah, in the presence of Hanamel my uncle’s son, and in the presence of the witnesses who signed the deed of the purchase, before all the Jews who sat in the court of the guard.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah gives the deed to Baruch son of Neriah before Hanamel, the witnesses, and all the Jews in the court of the guard. Arminians see the public nature of the act, which allowed many to witness this sign of hope.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see Baruch’s role as Jeremiah’s trusted scribe (compare 36:4). Both traditions note that the witnesses make the sign a public testimony, not a private act of faith.

verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah says he commanded Baruch in front of them all. Arminian readers see the prophet speaking openly, so that his instructions about the deed would be heard by everyone present.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as introducing the LORD’s command in the next verse. Both traditions note that Jeremiah’s instructions carry God’s authority, since what follows is the word of the LORD of Armies.

verses.text: the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says: ‘Take these deeds, this deed of the purchase which is sealed, and this deed which is open, and put them in an earthen vessel, that they may last many days.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies commands that the sealed and open deeds be put in a clay jar so they last many days. Arminians see a sign that looks far ahead, since the deeds must survive a long time before the promise is fulfilled.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the clay jar as a way of preserving documents. Both traditions read the instruction as showing that God’s promise is not immediate, but that it is certain enough to plan for.

verses.text: For the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel says: ‘Houses and fields and vineyards will yet again be bought in this land.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies says houses, fields, and vineyards will again be bought in this land. Arminian readers see the meaning of the sign: beyond the coming exile, God will restore normal life to his people in the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s faithfulness to his promises despite judgment. Both traditions treat this verse as shared ground about restoration, and they note that the promise is repeated in 32:43–44.
